title: Hours, Not Seconds, Not Days
subtitle: A man whose left ear keeps failing, from the third attack to the injection
description: Sorting vertigo by how long it lasts, reading a low-frequency audiogram, counting the criteria, which test rules out the tumor, first-line management and what not to give daily, and what to offer when attacks keep coming.

steps.title: Step 1/6: How Long It Lasts
steps.scenario:
A 62-year-old man, brought by his wife.

    Complaint       attacks of the room spinning
    Each attack     2 to 4 hours, with vomiting
    Afterward       a day of unsteadiness, then normal
    Frequency       2 or 3 a month, for a year
    Today           no attack

Left ear
    Tinnitus        roaring, most of the time
    Fullness        builds just before an attack
    Hearing         drops during attacks, partly comes back

Right ear         fine
Headache          none with attacks; no light or sound sensitivity

Past: admitted twice in 8 years for "sudden hearing loss" on the left, each time with vertigo, treated with steroids.
An emergency brain CT after one attack: normal.
steps.question: What does the time course tell you?

options.text: (A) Attacks lasting seconds with head position: benign paroxysmal positional vertigo
(B) One attack lasting days: vestibular neuritis
(C) Recurrent attacks lasting hours, with hearing, tinnitus and fullness in one ear that change around the attacks: the pattern of Meniere's disease, which needs a documented hearing loss to confirm
(D) Attacks of any length with headache: vestibular migraine

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: C

Duration sorts vertigo before anything else does.
• Seconds, brought on by turning over or looking up: BPPV.
• Minutes to hours, recurrent, with a normal ear between attacks and often a headache: vestibular migraine.
• Hours, recurrent, with hearing loss, tinnitus and fullness in one ear that fluctuate with the attacks: Meniere's disease.
• Days, a single continuous episode, hearing normal: vestibular neuritis.

His attacks last hours and come back, and his left ear tells the rest of the story: a roaring tinnitus, fullness that builds before an attack, hearing that drops and partly recovers. That is endolymphatic hydrops behaving as it does, and it is the clinical picture of Meniere's disease. What it is not yet is a diagnosis, because the criteria require the hearing loss to be documented on an audiogram, not just described.

The two admissions for sudden hearing loss are worth a second look. Sudden sensorineural loss with vertigo and roaring tinnitus that partly recovers, and then happens again in the same ear, is how Meniere's disease often first presents. Each admission treated an attack; nobody yet connected the attacks.

Why the others fail:
(A) BPPV lasts seconds to a minute and is positional. Hours of spinning with vomiting is not a canal problem.
(B) Vestibular neuritis is one attack lasting days, and it does not come back three times a month. His are recurrent and shorter.
(D) Vestibular migraine is the main alternative and must be asked about, but he has no headache, no photophobia or phonophobia with attacks, and migraine does not produce a fluctuating hearing loss in one ear.

Keypoint: hours, recurrent, one ear with fluctuating hearing, tinnitus and fullness: suspect Meniere's disease, and the next step is the audiogram that will confirm or refute it.

Reference: Lopez-Escamez JA, Carey J, Chung WH, et al. Diagnostic criteria for Meniere's disease. J Vestib Res. 2015;25(1):1-7. Basura GJ, Adams ME, Monfared A, et al. Clinical practice guideline: Meniere's disease. Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg. 2020;162(2_suppl):S1-S55. doi:10.1177/0194599820909438.

steps.title: Step 2/6: The Audiogram
steps.scenario:
Otoscopy          both drums normal
Weber             to the right
Rinne             normal, both sides

Audiogram today, between attacks:

    Left     250 Hz 55 / 500 Hz 50 / 1 kHz 45 / 2 kHz 30 / 4 kHz 25 / 8 kHz 25 dB HL
    Right    10 to 20 dB HL across
    Speech discrimination, left    72 percent
steps.media: Load image: Pure-tone audiogram from this patient, de-identified, unannotated. Caption: 'Audiogram, between attacks.'
steps.question: What is the pattern, and why does it matter?

options.text: (A) A rising, low-frequency sensorineural loss on the left, worst at 250 to 1000 Hz: the audiometric signature of endolymphatic hydrops, and the criterion that defines the affected ear
(B) A high-frequency loss on the left: noise damage from his work
(C) A flat loss on the left: the residue of his two sudden hearing losses, unrelated to the vertigo
(D) A conductive loss on the left, from fluid behind the drum

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: A

Most sensorineural losses slope downward: high frequencies go first, in age, in noise, in most ototoxicity. Meniere's disease does the opposite. The hydrops distorts the cochlear apex first, where the low frequencies are coded, so the early audiogram rises: worst at 250 to 1000 Hz, better toward 4000 and 8000. As the disease goes on the loss flattens and spreads, but in the first years the rising shape is the clue.

The Barany criteria make this the deciding criterion. Definite Meniere's disease requires a low- to mid-frequency sensorineural loss in one ear, documented on audiometry on at least one occasion, before, during or after an attack. His left ear, 55 dB at 250 Hz rising to 25 dB at 4 kHz, with a normal right ear, is that. The audiogram does two things: it confirms the diagnosis, and it names the ear.

The tuning forks agree: Weber to the right, the better cochlea, and Rinne normal on both sides. Sensorineural, left.

Why the others fail:
(B) Noise and age damage the high frequencies first. His high frequencies are the best part of his left ear. This is the reverse of a noise notch.
(C) The loss is not flat; it rises. And the two sudden losses were not unrelated to the vertigo: they were attacks of the same disease, and the residual low-frequency loss is what they left behind.
(D) Rinne is normal, the drum is normal, and Weber went to the other ear. Nothing here is conductive.

Keypoint: a rising, low-frequency sensorineural loss in one ear with episodic vertigo is Meniere's disease on paper; the audiogram both confirms it and says which ear.

Reference: Lopez-Escamez JA, Carey J, Chung WH, et al. J Vestib Res. 2015;25(1):1-7. Basura GJ, Adams ME, Monfared A, et al. Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg. 2020;162(2_suppl):S1-S55, Key Action Statement 3.

steps.title: Step 3/6: Definite or Probable
steps.scenario:
What you have:

    Vertigo           recurrent, spontaneous, 2 to 4 hours each, many in a year
    Hearing           low- to mid-frequency sensorineural loss, left, documented today
    Aural symptoms    left tinnitus, fullness and hearing that fluctuate with attacks
    Other cause       no headache or migraine features; no neurological signs; drums normal

The Barany Society criteria are shown.
steps.media: Load image: Your own table of the Barany Society 2015 criteria, redrawn: Definite = two or more spontaneous vertigo episodes of 20 minutes to 12 hours; audiometrically documented low- to mid-frequency sensorineural loss in one ear on at least one occasion before, during or after an episode; fluctuating aural symptoms in that ear; not better explained. Probable = two or more episodes of 20 minutes to 24 hours; fluctuating aural symptoms; not better explained. No row highlighted. Caption: 'Barany Society criteria, 2015.'
steps.question: Using the criteria shown, what is the diagnosis?

options.text: (A) Probable Meniere's disease, because the hearing loss was documented between attacks rather than during one
(B) Probable Meniere's disease, because an MRI has not yet excluded other causes
(C) Meniere's disease cannot be diagnosed without electrocochleography

(D) Definite Meniere's disease: two or more attacks of 20 minutes to 12 hours, audiometrically documented low- to mid-frequency loss in the affected ear, fluctuating aural symptoms in that ear, and no better explanation

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: D

The Barany Society criteria have two tiers, and the difference is the audiogram.

Definite Meniere's disease, all four:
1. Two or more spontaneous episodes of vertigo, each lasting 20 minutes to 12 hours.
2. Audiometrically documented low- to mid-frequency sensorineural hearing loss in one ear, defining the affected ear, on at least one occasion before, during or after an episode.
3. Fluctuating aural symptoms in the affected ear: hearing, tinnitus or fullness.
4. Not better accounted for by another vestibular diagnosis.

Probable Meniere's disease: two or more episodes of 20 minutes to 24 hours, fluctuating aural symptoms in the affected ear, and no better explanation. No documented hearing loss required.

He meets all four for definite. The audiogram does not have to be taken during an attack; the criterion says before, during or after, on at least one occasion, and today's is enough for the diagnosis.

One audiogram is the threshold, not the whole practice. A single test shows that a low-frequency loss exists and names the ear; it cannot show that the loss fluctuates, and so far the fluctuation rests on his history. Serial audiograms over the next visits do three things the first one cannot: they document the fluctuation objectively, they track the drift toward a flatter, fixed loss as the disease matures, and they watch the other ear, which becomes involved in a minority of patients over the years. The diagnosis is made today; the natural history is made over time. The fourth criterion is the one that asks you to think: the alternative that mimics this best is vestibular migraine, which is why the headache questions in Step 1 mattered, and the structural cause that must be excluded is a tumor on the nerve, which is Step 4.

Why the others fail:
(A) The criterion accepts an audiogram before, during or after an episode. Between attacks counts. A hearing loss that persists between attacks is, if anything, stronger evidence.
(B) The criteria are clinical. MRI is done to exclude a schwannoma, and it is the next step, but its absence does not downgrade a diagnosis that meets all four criteria.
(C) Electrocochleography is not part of the criteria and the guideline says not to use it to establish the diagnosis. It has a research role and is inconsistent in practice.

Keypoint: two attacks of 20 minutes to 12 hours, a documented low-frequency loss naming the ear, fluctuating aural symptoms, nothing else to explain it: definite.

Reference: Lopez-Escamez JA, Carey J, Chung WH, et al. Diagnostic criteria for Meniere's disease. J Vestib Res. 2015;25(1):1-7. Basura GJ, Adams ME, Monfared A, et al. Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg. 2020;162(2_suppl):S1-S55, Key Action Statements 1, 2 and 5.

steps.title: Step 4/6: The Test That Matters
steps.scenario:
Definite Meniere's disease, left.

He asks what other tests he needs.
He mentions the emergency brain CT was normal and asks whether that settles it.
steps.media: Load image: Axial T1 post-contrast MRI through the internal auditory canals from this patient, de-identified, unannotated. Caption: 'MRI, internal auditory canals.'
steps.question: Which investigation do you order, and which do you not?

options.text: (A) Caloric testing and electrocochleography, to confirm the hydrops objectively
(B) MRI of the internal auditory canals and posterior fossa with gadolinium, to exclude a vestibular schwannoma behind an asymmetric sensorineural loss; no routine vestibular testing, no repeat CT
(C) Nothing; the normal CT already excluded a tumor
(D) CT of the temporal bones with contrast

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: B

One investigation changes management, and it is the one that looks for the thing Meniere's disease can hide.

MRI. A vestibular schwannoma presents with an asymmetric sensorineural loss, tinnitus, and sometimes episodic vertigo. It can mimic Meniere's disease for years. The guideline says to offer MRI of the internal auditory canals and posterior fossa, with gadolinium, to any patient with an asymmetric sensorineural loss, and he has one. The scan does not confirm Meniere's disease; it clears the differential that matters. His was normal, which is what most are.

What not to order routinely:
• Vestibular function tests. Calorics, video head impulse and VEMPs describe how much function the left ear has lost. That is useful later, when deciding on an ablative treatment or when the diagnosis is in doubt, but the guideline says not to use them to make the diagnosis.
• Electrocochleography. An elevated summating-to-action-potential ratio suggests hydrops, but the test is inconsistent and the guideline says not to use it to establish the diagnosis.
• CT. It does not show the nerve or the labyrinth's contents. The emergency department CT was the right test for a stroke question at 2 a.m.; it is the wrong test for this question and does not need repeating.

Why the others fail:
(A) Neither test is part of the diagnostic criteria, and the guideline recommends against ordering either routinely to make the diagnosis. They do not exclude a tumor.
(C) A normal brain CT does not exclude a schwannoma in the internal auditory canal. Small ones are invisible on CT.
(D) Temporal bone CT shows bone. The lesion you are excluding is soft tissue in the canal and the cerebellopontine angle, and MRI is the test.

Keypoint: asymmetric sensorineural loss gets an MRI of the internal auditory canals; vestibular testing and ECochG are not how the diagnosis is made, and a normal CT excludes nothing.

Reference: Basura GJ, Adams ME, Monfared A, et al. Clinical practice guideline: Meniere's disease. Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg. 2020;162(2_suppl):S1-S55, Key Action Statements 4, 5 and 6.

steps.title: Step 5/6: What to Start
steps.scenario:
MRI normal. Definite Meniere's disease, left.

Audiogram, repeated ten days after an attack:

    Left     250 Hz 70 / 500 Hz 65 / 1 kHz 55 / 2 kHz 35 / 4 kHz 25 / 8 kHz 25 dB HL
    Right    unchanged

Compared with the first audiogram, the low frequencies are 10 to 15 dB worse and the high frequencies are the same.

    Attacks        2 or 3 a month
    Current drug   diphenidol every day, since his last emergency visit; he is afraid of the next attack

He asks whether there is anything better.
steps.media: Load image: The two audiograms from this patient side by side, between attacks and ten days after an attack, de-identified, unannotated. Caption: 'Audiograms, between attacks and after an attack.'
steps.question: What do you start, and what do you stop?

options.text: (A) Continue daily diphenidol and add a daily benzodiazepine
(B) A course of oral corticosteroid with each attack, as for sudden hearing loss

(C) Education and lifestyle: salt and caffeine restriction, sleep, stress; a trial of a diuretic or betahistine for prevention; a vestibular suppressant and antiemetic kept for attacks only, and the daily diphenidol stopped
(D) Intratympanic gentamicin now, to stop the attacks for good

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: C

First, the second audiogram. The low frequencies have moved 10 to 15 dB and the high frequencies have not. That is the fluctuation the criteria describe, now on paper rather than in his account, and it is the pattern to keep tracking at each visit: how far the low frequencies swing, and whether they stop swinging and settle into a fixed loss.

Meniere's disease is managed in tiers, and the first tier is not a drug.

Education. What the disease is, that it comes in attacks and remissions, that most people are controlled without invasive treatment, and that the hearing in the affected ear will probably decline over years regardless. The guideline lists this as a recommendation, not an option.

Lifestyle. Sodium restriction, less caffeine and alcohol, regular sleep, attention to stress. The evidence is weak but the cost is nothing, and some patients find their triggers.

Prevention, as an option. A diuretic such as hydrochlorothiazide, or betahistine. The evidence for both is thin and the guideline grades them as options, not recommendations. A trial for a few months is reasonable; if attacks do not fall, stop.

Rescue, for the attack itself. A vestibular suppressant such as diphenidol or a benzodiazepine, with an antiemetic, taken when an attack starts and stopped when it ends. This is the correction that matters most today: suppressants taken every day do not prevent attacks, they sedate him between them, and in a disease where the brain needs to compensate for a fluctuating ear they delay that compensation. The guideline says they are for acute attacks only.

Vestibular rehabilitation is for the chronic imbalance some patients develop between attacks, not for the attacks themselves.

Why the others fail:
(A) Daily suppressants sedate without preventing and hold back compensation. Adding a second one compounds it.
(B) Oral steroids are for a sudden sensorineural loss. Once the diagnosis is Meniere's disease, a steroid course with each of thirty attacks a year is harm without evidence.
(D) Gentamicin destroys the vestibular function of the ear and carries a real risk to its hearing. It is for attacks that have failed non-ablative treatment, not for a patient who has not yet had any.

Keypoint: educate, restrict salt and caffeine, try a diuretic or betahistine, keep the suppressant for attacks and stop it between them.

Reference: Basura GJ, Adams ME, Monfared A, et al. Clinical practice guideline: Meniere's disease. Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg. 2020;162(2_suppl):S1-S55, Key Action Statements 7, 8 and 13.

steps.title: Step 6/6: When the Attacks Keep Coming
steps.scenario:
Six months later.

    Done           salt and caffeine restriction; hydrochlorothiazide; daily diphenidol stopped
    Attacks        still 2 a month, 3 to 4 hours each
    Hearing, left  low-frequency loss, slightly worse; discrimination 68 percent
    Hearing, right normal
    Work           installs solar panels on roofs; has stopped climbing

He asks what comes next.
steps.media: Load image: Endoscopic photograph from your own clinic, de-identified: intratympanic injection, needle through the posteroinferior quadrant of the drum. Caption: 'Intratympanic injection.'
steps.question: What do you offer?

options.text: (A) Intratympanic corticosteroid, a non-ablative step that reduces attack frequency in many patients without risking the hearing; gentamicin held in reserve if it fails
(B) Intratympanic gentamicin as the first injection, since it is more effective
(C) Double the diuretic and review in another six months
(D) Positive pressure therapy through a ventilation tube

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: A

He has failed the first tier, and the failure matters more than usual because he works on roofs. The guideline's next tier is intratympanic, and it is ordered by what each drug costs the ear.

Intratympanic corticosteroid. Dexamethasone or methylprednisolone injected through the drum, absorbed across the round window. It can be repeated, and it does not damage hearing or vestibular function. Its benefit should be described honestly: attack frequency falls in many patients, but the effect is modest and the trials are small, and the placebo arms of the injection trials in this disease improve too, which is a reminder that Meniere's disease remits on its own. In the one double-blind head-to-head trial, methylprednisolone and gentamicin gave similar vertigo control at two years, with no hearing cost from the steroid. It is the non-ablative option, and the guideline says it may be offered to patients whose attacks are not controlled by non-invasive treatment. That is him.

Intratympanic gentamicin. A vestibulotoxic aminoglycoside that ablates the vestibular function of the injected ear. Vertigo control is high, around nine in ten, but the drug also reaches the cochlea: pooled estimates put some hearing reduction in roughly a quarter of patients and a profound loss in a few percent, depending on the dosing protocol. The guideline says to offer it to patients who have failed non-ablative therapy. His hearing on the left is damaged but still useful, with 68 percent discrimination, and that is worth protecting for as long as possible. Gentamicin is the step after steroid fails, not instead of it.

Beyond that lie the surgical options, from endolymphatic sac procedures to labyrinthectomy, each with its own place, and each for a patient who has been through the steps above.

Why the others fail:
(B) More effective at stopping vertigo, at the price of the ear's balance function and a real risk to its hearing. Ablation is for the patient who has failed the non-ablative injection, and he has not had it yet.
(C) The diuretic evidence is weak at the standard dose; a higher dose adds electrolyte risk, not efficacy, and six more months on a roof with two attacks a month is not acceptable.
(D) The guideline recommends against positive pressure therapy. The trials did not show benefit over placebo.

Keypoint: attacks that survive diet and a diuretic go to intratympanic steroid first, because it does not cost the ear anything; gentamicin is the ablative step for when that fails.

Reference: Basura GJ, Adams ME, Monfared A, et al. Clinical practice guideline: Meniere's disease. Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg. 2020;162(2_suppl):S1-S55, Key Action Statements 9, 10 and 11. Patel M, Agarwal K, Arshad Q, et al. Intratympanic methylprednisolone versus gentamicin in patients with unilateral Meniere's disease: a randomised, double-blind, comparative effectiveness trial. Lancet. 2016;388(10061):2753-2762. Webster KE, Lee A, Galbraith K, et al. Intratympanic corticosteroids for Meniere's disease. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2023. Complete citation.
